newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - NJTransit sees more energy savings.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NJTransit sees more energy savings.

text.p: New Jersey Transit Corp is looking to electric utility deregulation to expand its energy savings, Steven Clark told Reuters.
At the same time, the state commuter agency is getting ready for its second round of natural gas bids, he said.

As manager of management engineering projects, Clark is responsible for NJTransit's electricity, natural gas and diesel fuel purchases. The agency's biggest use of electricity is traction power for commuter trains, while some trains and its buses are diesel-fueled, and gas is used for heating.
"Our challenge is putting together specifications" so NJTransit and other state agencies will be ready to accept bids when the power market is deregulated, Clark said.
Under regulations proposed by New Jersey's Board of Public Utilities, deregulation will come faster for state agencies than for other electricity users, he pointed out.

Under its Final Report adopted in March, the board called for 10 percent of each utility's total load to be opened to competition by October 1, 1998. This rises in stages to 75 percent on April 1, 2000, and 100 percent July 1, 2000.
The proposal then said "each block of the phase will be expanded by an additional 5 percent to accommodate municipal aggregation and state and county entities."

"This (5 percent expansion) is how we get in early," Clark said. He noted the board's Final Report speeded 100 percent deregulation up by nine months, brining closer to the views expressed by NJTransit.
He expects the power purchase specifications to be similar to the natural gas specifications developed by NJTransit and adopted by the New Jersey's Treasurer for state-wide use.
The natural gas specifications call for a commodity price to be locked in on the New York Mercantile Exchange and the marketer to provide bundled delivery services, Clark said.
This is really a rebundling of services, he pointed out.
NJTransit has purchased its diesel fuel through two-oil commodity contracts for nearly a decade at a cost now running about $19 million a year, Clark said.
The first, two-year gas contract went to Norstar in November 1995, giving NJTransit a delivered price of $0.18 per therm and "saving (the agency) over $500,000 a year," he said.

Earlier this month, Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc said it is ending Norstar operations after selling the marketing partnership's assets to UGI Corp. Norstar reduced first half earnings $0.83 per share, the utility said.
Prior to the sale, an Orange & Rockland spokesman said, the company bought out its Norstar partner -- Shell Gas Trading Co -- for undisclosed terms.
Like the gas contract now in effect, the pact to be negotiated this fall will provide heat for bus garages.
In two years, Clark said, natural gas will also be purchased for use in buses fueled with compressed gas.

Clark said the agency's traction power bill has already has already been reduced $700,000 per year through renegotiation of GPU Inc's tariffs, and he expects Amtrak to pass through "a substantial portion" of its 30 percent savings under a new contract with Enron Corp.

Once that contract becomes effective, Clark said, Amtrak will go from being NJTransint's most expensive power supplier to being its cheapest source of electricity, leaving Public Service Electric & Gas as the most costly.
With full retail wheeling, he said, NJTransit expects to reduce its power costs to $0.06 to $0.07 per kilowatt hour from the present average of about $0.083.
He stressed the "about" noting payments to Amtrak are "calculated on a car mile basis," rather than kilowatts used.
He said NJTransit now pays about $30 million per year for electricity, including $13 million paid to Amtrak.
The agency estimates deregulation would reduce the $17 million now paid PSE&G and GPU each year about $2.5 to $5 million. ((-- New York Newsdesk 212 859-1610))
